meta.audience: Lamoni's household and the gathered multitude
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)

world_behind.title: The burial clock was running
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has the household two days and two nights into mourning and ready to lay the king in a sepulchre they had prepared. The chapter opens at the last hour when anything could still be done.

world_behind.title: The queen holds the household together
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says she had heard of Ammon's fame and sent for him herself. The king is unconscious, the servants are frightened, and the decision about the body is hers.

world_behind.title: Abish had been a believer for years
world_behind.text: Verse 16 says she was converted on account of a remarkable vision of her father, and verse 17 says she had never made it known. The record introduces her at the moment her silence ends.

world_behind.title: A blood feud was still open
world_behind.text: Verse 21 identifies the men who had scattered the flocks at Sebus, and verse 22 has the brother of a man Ammon killed drawing a sword in the king's own house. The crowd that gathers is not neutral.

world_behind.title: The Great Spirit was the available category
world_behind.text: Verses 25 through 27 show the people reaching for the term Lamoni used in Alma 18, and reaching different conclusions with it. A shared vocabulary produced three incompatible readings of the same scene.

world_behind.title: Ammon's survival was promised in advance
world_behind.text: Verse 23 reaches back to Mosiah 28, where the Lord told Mosiah he would deliver his sons out of Lamanite hands. Mormon inserts the promise at the exact verse where a sword came down.

world_behind.title: The church begins here
world_behind.text: Verse 35 has believers baptized and a church established among the Lamanites, and verse 36 calls it the commencement of the work. Everything in Alma 20 through 26 grows out of this room.

words.text: A hewn burial chamber rather than a grave in the ground. The record uses the word four times: twice here, of the tomb prepared for Lamoni, and twice earlier of the Messiah's own burial in 1 Nephi 19 and 2 Nephi 25. A Lamanite king is about to be laid in the only kind of place this book has so far reserved for Christ, and he gets up instead.

Gives off the smell of decay. It occurs once in this record and twice in the King James Bible, and one of those is Martha at the mouth of Lazarus's tomb. The queen uses the word to report what other people are saying and then denies it in her own voice.

A hanging cloth, and by extension anything that blocks sight. Six of the record's seven occurrences sit in Ether, where the veil is something a man passes through to see the Lord. Here alone the veil belongs to the man himself: "the dark veil of unbelief" (v. 6) is being taken off Lamoni's mind while he lies still.

Present tense of sleep, used of a body that looks dead. The word appears once in this record and seven times in the King James Bible, and two of those are Jesus saying it of Jairus's daughter and of Lazarus. Ammon reaches for the exact vocabulary of the raising accounts, in front of a woman who has never read one.

Stretched full length on the ground, face down. It occurs three times in scripture, all three in Alma, and never in the King James Bible. Two are in this chapter, describing the household on the floor. The third is Lamoni's father in Alma 22, in the same posture, two chapters later.

Something unnatural and dangerous. The record uses it six times and the King James Bible never. Three occurrences are Jacob's phrase for death and hell in 2 Nephi 9, one is the sea in Ether 6, and this is the only time anyone applies it to a person. A crowd looking at a sleeping man calls the missionary the monster.

phrases.term: Some say that he is not dead, but others say that he is dead
phrases.text: The queen reports the household split before she asks for anything. She has no ruling of her own to give, and she says so. Her honesty about the disagreement is what makes her next sentence carry weight.

phrases.term: But as for myself, to me he doth not stink
phrases.text: A woman's private evidence against the consensus of a household. She has been in the room, and she trusts her own senses over the report of people who want the burial to proceed. The claim is small, physical, and correct.

phrases.term: The dark veil of unbelief was being cast away from his mind
phrases.text: Mormon tells the reader what is happening inside a man who looks comatose. The verse is the only window in the chapter into Lamoni's experience, and it describes removal rather than addition. Light comes in once the covering is off.

phrases.term: He is not dead, but he sleepeth in God
phrases.text: Ammon gives a diagnosis and a timetable in one breath, then a command: bury him not. He is staking his credibility on a body rising by morning. The queen has to decide what to do with a stranger's medical opinion about her husband.

phrases.term: I have had no witness save thy word, and the word of our servants
phrases.text: The queen states exactly how thin her evidence is. She has hearsay from her staff and an assertion from a foreigner, and nothing else. She names the poverty of her grounds and believes anyway, and the naming is what Ammon praises.

phrases.term: There has not been such great faith among all the people of the Nephites
phrases.text: Ammon ranks a Lamanite queen above his entire nation. He has been raised to think of these people as the problem, and within days of arriving he says the best faith he has ever seen belongs to one of them.

phrases.term: Having been converted to the Lord, and never having made it known
phrases.text: Two clauses that hold years between them. Abish believed on account of her father's vision, kept working in the house of a king who executed servants, and told no one. The record states the fact without judging it and then shows what her one action sets loose.

phrases.term: He was a monster, who had been sent from the Nephites to torment them
phrases.text: The worst available reading of Ammon, offered by people with real grievances. He had killed their brothers at Sebus. The chapter lets the accusation stand in the crowd's own words before the queen wakes up and answers it by praising Jesus.

phrases.term: O blessed Jesus, who has saved me from an awful hell
phrases.text: The first words out of the queen's mouth, spoken to a room mid-riot. She names Jesus, which nobody in the chapter has taught her, and her second sentence asks mercy for the people who were arguing over her body.

verses.label: v. 28–30
verses.title: The raising runs through touch, twice
verses.text: Abish takes the queen by the hand and she rises; the queen takes the king by the hand and he rises. By the hand appears in these two verses and nowhere else in the chapter. What breaks the paralysis is not a word but a grip, passed along by the one person who never fell.

verses.label: v. 29–30
verses.title: The record notes speech it cannot report
verses.text: After the cry about an awful hell, the queen clasps her hands, "speaking many words which were not understood." The account admits a gap in itself rather than filling it, and then moves straight on to the next hand taken.

verses.label: v. 31–33
verses.title: The outcome is split, and the testimony is uniform
verses.text: Many hear Lamoni and believe; "but there were many among them who would not hear his words; therefore they went their way." The record claims no triumph and prints the refusal in the same breath as the belief. What it does claim is agreement among the witnesses: they all declared "the selfsame thing," that their hearts had been changed and they had no more desire to do evil.

chapter.title: The chapter turns on three women
chapter.text: The queen sends for Ammon and believes without a witness. Abish gathers the crowd and lifts the queen by the hand. The king, the missionary, and every male servant spend the middle of the chapter unconscious on the floor.

chapter.title: Faith is praised for naming its own thinness
chapter.text: The queen tells Ammon she has only his word and her servants' word. That admission is the thing he calls exceeding faith. Belief here is treated as a decision made in the open about insufficient evidence.

chapter.title: Abish's twenty years are left unexplained
chapter.text: The record gives her conversion, her father's vision, her silence, and her name, and no account of why she waited. Readers get one verse of backstory for the only Lamanite woman the book names.

chapter.title: Her plan misfires and works anyway
chapter.text: Verse 17 gives her reasoning, that she "knew that it was the power of God" and ran to gather a crowd. Verse 28 reports the result, "the contention began to be exceedingly sharp among them," and that she "was exceedingly sorrowful, even unto tears." What she did next was physical rather than persuasive: verse 29 has her take the queen by the hand. The believing begins after the queen speaks at verse 29 and the king at verse 30, which is nothing she planned.

chapter.title: The crowd's readings are all religious
chapter.text: Great evil, divine punishment for the slain servants, the Great Spirit himself, a monster sent to torment. Nobody in the multitude suggests a natural cause. Shared vocabulary about God did not narrow the field at all.

chapter.title: Conversion arrives in the body
chapter.text: Six people are flat on the ground for most of the chapter, and the record treats this as what the Spirit poured out looks like from outside. The queen's testimony comes out of her the second she is on her feet.

chapter.title: A promise made in Zarahemla holds in Ishmael
chapter.text: Verse 23 breaks the action mid-scene to quote a promise made in another book: "the Lord had said unto Mosiah, his father: I will spare him, and it shall be unto him according to thy faith." The reason given for the survival is not Ammon's strength but a father's faith recorded at Mosiah 28:6–7. The record thus reaches back two books and one country to explain why a raised sword did not fall.

chapter.title: The church is founded out of a riot
chapter.text: Verse 35 reports baptisms and a church established, and verse 36 states the general conclusion, "his arm is extended to all people who will repent and believe on his name." Both follow from the crowd assembled at verse 17 by one servant woman, named at verse 16 as Abish and described as "converted unto the Lord for many years" without anyone knowing. A national church begins in a riot started by a woman whose conversion the record says was secret until that afternoon.

applications.title: Say what you actually saw
applications.text: The queen reports her evidence and its source, "The servants of my husband have made it known unto me," and then states the disagreement plainly, "some say that he is not dead." She does not overclaim and she does not wait for certainty before acting.

applications.title: Name how thin your grounds are, then act
applications.text: Asked whether she believes, she answers exactly, "I have had no witness save thy word, and the word of our servants; nevertheless I believe." The admission and the belief are in one sentence, and verse 10 calls it great faith.

applications.title: Ask the question before you make the promise
applications.text: Ammon asks "Believest thou this?" before he says anything about what will happen. Getting the person to say where they stand is part of the work and not a preliminary to it.

applications.title: Stop keeping it to yourself
applications.text: Abish had been converted "for many years" and had never made it known, and the record says so twice. What ended the secrecy was a situation only she could read. Something you have been quiet about may be the thing a moment needs.

applications.title: Read the reason for the survival back
applications.text: The record interrupts the raised sword to quote a promise made to a father in another country, "I will spare him, and it shall be unto him according to thy faith." When you come through something, it is worth asking whose earlier work you were standing in.

applications.title: Expect the first result to be an argument
applications.text: What Abish produced was contention "exceedingly sharp," not belief, and she wept over it. The good outcome at verse 35 comes later and through somebody else. A right action does not always produce its result in your hands.

applications.title: Use your hands when words are not working
applications.text: In the middle of the quarrel she takes the queen by the hand, and the queen then takes the king by the hand. Two physical acts move the scene where the arguing could not.

applications.title: Say the thing you heard from somebody else
applications.text: Lamoni rebukes the crowd by teaching them "the words which he had heard from the mouth of Ammon." Passing on what you were told, in the words you were told it in, is a real contribution and does not require originality.

questions.text: Who am I in a position to send for, and have I?
When have I trusted the crowd's report over what I could see myself?
What do I believe on evidence I would be embarrassed to describe out loud?
Whose faith have I been slow to admit is better than mine?
What have I been converted to and never made known?
What grievance am I still carrying that would make me swing at the wrong person?
If I were raised up mid-argument, what would come out of my mouth first?
